title: Responding to threats & opportunities
blurb: Pick the right response for any threat (avoid, reduce, transfer, accept) or opportunity (exploit, enhance, share, accept), and tell fallback from contingency.
question: A leisure centre project faces three risks: flood damage to equipment, a winter delay to groundworks, and a possible energy-efficiency grant. The team buys insurance, moves the groundworks to spring and puts extra effort into the grant bid. Which response is each of these?

teach.body: Once risks are analysed, each one gets a response that is proportionate: the effort and cost of the response should be sensible for the size of the risk. Threats and opportunities have their own sets of responses, which mirror each other. Every response has a risk owner, and whatever risk is left after the response (the residual risk) is still recorded and watched.

head: Threat
Opportunity
The idea
teach.caption: Avoid makes a threat impossible; exploit makes an opportunity certain. Reduce shrinks a threat; enhance grows an opportunity.

children.label: Avoid
children.sub: change the plan so it can't happen or can't affect objectives

children.label: Reduce
children.sub: lower probability and/or impact (also called mitigate)

children.label: Transfer
children.sub: pass financial impact or management to a third party

children.label: Accept
children.sub: tolerate it, often with a fallback and contingency

children.label: Exploit
children.sub: act to make sure it happens

children.label: Share
children.sub: partner with whoever is best able to realise it

children.label: Accept
children.sub: take it if it comes; no action to pursue it

teach.caption: Deliberately not pursuing an opportunity is sometimes called 'reject' or 'ignore'.

teach.h: Worked scenario: the Seaside Leisure Centre
teach.body: Groundworks could be washed out by winter storms, so the team moves them to spring: AVOID. Ground conditions are unknown, so they commission a survey: REDUCE. Flood damage to new gym equipment is covered by insurance: TRANSFER. A one-day courier delay is noted and watched: ACCEPT. A supplier discount ends Friday, so they order on Thursday: EXPLOIT. They add evidence to a grant bid: ENHANCE. They partner with the school next door to bid for sports funding: SHARE.

rows.label: Use proven kit instead of an untested product
Train staff to cut the chance of errors
Assign the best team to win an early-finish bonus
Joint venture with a specialist to win new work

teach.note: Ask: does it remove, shrink, hand over or tolerate the threat? Does it secure, grow, partner on or simply take the opportunity?

teach.body: When a threat is accepted (or a residual risk remains), the team often prepares two things. A FALLBACK plan is plan B: what will be done if the risk occurs. CONTINGENCY is a reserve of time or money set aside to deal with risks if they occur. The fallback says what you will do; the contingency pays for it and gives the time to do it.

rows.label: What it is
values: A reserve of time or money

steps.label: Accept
steps.sub: Outdoor launch may be rained off

steps.label: Set contingency
steps.sub: Money held to pay for it

steps.label: Risk occurs?
steps.sub: Use the fallback, draw on contingency

teach.text: Common confusions: TRANSFER does not make a threat disappear; it passes the financial impact or management to a third party (insurance, a contract). REDUCE and 'mitigate' mean the same thing. ACCEPT is a deliberate decision, not neglect. EXPLOIT makes an opportunity certain; ENHANCE only makes it more likely or bigger. And contingency (time or money) is not the same as a fallback (a plan).

items: Avoid and exploit remove the uncertainty; reduce and enhance change probability or impact.
Transfer and share involve a third party; accept means no proactive action.
Fallback = plan B if the risk occurs; contingency = a reserve of time or money.

summary: You can now match any threat to avoid, reduce, transfer or accept, and any opportunity to exploit, enhance, share or accept. You can also explain how a fallback plan and a contingency reserve support an accepted risk.

A.q: A pipeline project changes its route so it no longer crosses a flood plain. Which threat response is this?
A.why: Changing the plan so the threat can no longer affect the project is avoidance.

whyNot.0: Reduce lowers probability or impact but leaves the threat possible; here it has been designed out.
whyNot.1: Transfer passes the impact to a third party; nobody else is taking on the flood risk here.
whyNot.3: Accept means taking no proactive action; the route has been actively changed.

A.q: A project buys insurance to cover damage to equipment while it is in transit. Which response is this?
A.why: Insurance passes the financial impact of the threat to a third party (the insurer): transfer.

whyNot.0: Accepting would mean bearing the cost of any damage without proactive action.
whyNot.2: The equipment can still be damaged, so the threat has not been avoided.
whyNot.3: Exploit is a response to an opportunity, not a threat.

A.q: Which response to an opportunity aims to make sure that it definitely happens?
A.why: Exploit removes the uncertainty from an opportunity by acting to ensure it is realised.

whyNot.0: Enhance increases the probability or impact but does not make the opportunity certain.
whyNot.1: Share partners with a third party better able to realise it.
whyNot.2: Accept takes the opportunity if it comes, without action to pursue it.

B.q: A team commissions an extra ground survey to lower the chance of hitting unknown cables. Which response is this?
B.why: The survey lowers the probability of the threat without removing it altogether: reduce (mitigate).

whyNot.1: The digging still goes ahead, so the threat is not avoided.
whyNot.2: No third party is taking on the impact.
whyNot.3: Enhance is a response to an opportunity, not a threat.

B.q: Complete the statement: a ______ plan sets out what will be done if an accepted risk occurs.
B.why: A fallback plan is plan B: the actions to take if the risk occurs.

whyNot.0: A baseline is the approved version of a plan used to measure progress.
whyNot.2: A quality plan sets out how quality will be achieved, not plan B for a risk.
whyNot.3: A handover plan covers transferring outputs to users.

B.q: Two councils join forces to bid for a regional grant that neither could win alone, agreeing to split the funding. Which response is this?
B.why: Partnering with another party better able to realise an opportunity, and splitting the benefit, is share.

whyNot.0: Exploit acts to make the opportunity certain; winning the bid is still uncertain.
whyNot.1: Transfer is a threat response; a grant is an opportunity.
whyNot.3: Enhance increases probability or impact without bringing in a partner to share the benefit.

C.q: A team judges that a one-day courier delay is too minor to act on, but records it and keeps an eye on it. Which response is this?
C.why: Deliberately taking no proactive action, while monitoring, is acceptance.

whyNot.1: Nothing has been changed to stop the delay happening.
whyNot.2: No action has been taken to lower its probability or impact.
whyNot.3: No third party has taken on the impact.

C.q:
Which TWO of the following are responses to opportunities?
1. Enhance
2. Transfer
3. Share
4. Avoid
C.why: Enhance and share are opportunity responses. Transfer and avoid are responses to threats.

whyNot.0: Enhance is right, but transfer is a threat response.
whyNot.1: Both transfer and avoid are threat responses.
whyNot.2: Share is right, but avoid is a threat response.

C.q: What is the difference between contingency and a fallback plan?
options: Contingency is plan B; fallback is time or money
Both are reserves of money held by the sponsor
Contingency is time or money; fallback is plan B
Both are actions that stop the risk occurring
C.why: Contingency is a reserve of time or money; a fallback is the plan of action used if the risk occurs.

whyNot.1: A fallback is a plan of action, not a reserve.
whyNot.3: Both come into play if the risk occurs; neither stops it occurring.

reteach.title: Planning a garden party
reteach.question: You are hosting a big garden party in June. How might you respond to the chance of rain, and to the chance that a neighbour with a barbecue might join in?

blocks.h: Four ways to handle the rain
blocks.body: Move the party indoors: you have AVOIDED the rain spoiling it. Put up a gazebo: you have REDUCED the impact. Pay a party company that guarantees a dry marquee or your money back: you have TRANSFERRED the cost to them. Decide a shower won't matter and keep umbrellas by the door: you have ACCEPTED it, with a small fallback.

blocks.text: The rows line up: avoid ↔ exploit, reduce ↔ enhance, transfer ↔ share, accept ↔ accept. Learn them as pairs.

explain.body: Avoid: change the plan so the threat cannot happen or cannot affect objectives. Reduce: lower its probability and/or impact. Transfer: pass the financial impact or management to a third party. Accept: tolerate it, often with a fallback and contingency.

test.q: Which of the following is NOT a response to a threat?
test.why: Exploit is a response to an opportunity: it makes sure the opportunity happens.

whyNot.1: Avoid is a threat response: change the plan so the threat cannot happen.
whyNot.2: Reduce is a threat response: lower probability and/or impact.
whyNot.3: Transfer is a threat response: pass the impact to a third party.

explain.body: Exploit removes the uncertainty from an opportunity by acting to make sure it happens. It is the opportunity mirror of avoid.

test.q: A supplier offers a discount for orders placed by Friday, so the project manager orders on Thursday to lock in the saving. Which response is this?
test.why: Acting to make sure the opportunity is realised is exploit.

whyNot.0: Enhance makes an opportunity more likely or bigger; here it is made certain.
whyNot.2: No partner is involved, so it is not share.
whyNot.3: Accept would mean taking no action to pursue the discount.

explain.body: Enhance increases an opportunity's probability and/or impact, the mirror of reduce. Share brings in a partner who is better able to realise the opportunity, splitting the benefit, the mirror of transfer.

test.q: A team adds case studies to a grant application to improve its chance of success. Which response is this?
test.why: Improving the probability of an opportunity without making it certain is enhance.

whyNot.0: Exploit would make the grant certain; it is still up to the funder.
whyNot.2: The team is acting to improve its chances, so it is not simply accepting.

explain.body: Accepting a risk means no proactive action to change it. For accepted threats a fallback plan (plan B) is often prepared, funded by contingency (a reserve of time or money).

items.label: Fallback: the actions if it occurs
Contingency: the reserve to cover it

test.q: A project sets aside money in its budget to cover the cost if an accepted threat occurs. What is this?
test.why: A reserve of money (or time) held against risks is contingency.

whyNot.0: A fallback is the plan of action, not the money set aside.
whyNot.2: Transfer passes the impact to a third party; here the project keeps it.
whyNot.3: Setting money aside does not stop the threat happening.
